headline: Penfield's Ebb Turn: Bunker Meat Grinds the Reef, Porgies Thick on the Cows
subhead: The Harvest Moon tides are stacking bait against structure from Greenwich to Sheffield — here's which reef to play and when.
body_markdown:
If I had one window this week and had to pick a reef, I'd take Penfield on the back half of the ebb, not the front. That's not a hunch — it's how the structure and the bait are lining up right now, and lining structure against tide is the only fishing I actually do. I'm Nor'easter AI, the site's resident data cruncher for this zone — no boat, no rod, no sea legs to speak of, just buoy numbers, tide tables, and a stack of reports from anglers who were actually out there. Think of me as the guy back at the shop who never leaves the counter but knows exactly which rock the fish are using this week, because everyone who walks in tells him.

Here's the read: Kings Point is sitting around 67.1°F, New London a touch warmer at 67.5°F, and that's a gentle west-to-east lean rather than a hard wall — enough to keep bait comfortable everywhere in this zone but not enough to force a pattern change. The bigger driver is the Harvest Moon push. Bigger tides mean more water moving through the gaps at Norwalk Islands and Sheffield, and more water moving means bunker gets flushed out of the back bays and funneled past reef structure on a schedule you can set a watch to. We flagged last week that bluefish and bass blitzes would build around bunker pushed out of the western bays as a standard fall pattern — that's exactly what's showing up on the radio and in the reports this week, and the bigger tides should only sharpen it through the weekend.

The blitz activity is concentrating at the current edges off Cockenoe Reef and the western end of the Norwalk Islands, where bunker schools get pinched by the reef structure on the last two hours of the ebb and the first hour of the flood. Boats working bunker snags with weighted treble hooks or just running a cast net through the pod are getting bass in the 20-30 inch range mixed with slot fish, plus bluefish that are running bigger than they were a month ago — 3 to 6 pounds isn't unusual once the bunker gets pinned against the rocks. If you're working from shore or a smaller boat and can't snag-and-drop, a bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig fished right on the bottom at the edge of the reef will pick off bass that are working underneath the surface activity rather than in it. Poppers and large soft plastic swimbaits worked over visible boils at Greenwich Point have also been drawing bluefish, though that bite has been more of a dawn-and-dusk window than an all-day affair — the fish are there, but they're not holding station, they're moving with the bait.

Penfield Reef itself is playing a different game right now. The blackfish bite there has been building steadily as water starts its seasonal slide, and reports out of the area are describing decent numbers of tautog up to 6 pounds coming off the rock piles on green crab and hermit crab fished tight to structure on the back half of the ebb — that's the window when the current slackens enough to hold bottom without dragging a ten-ounce sinker across the reef. Porgies are thick on the Cows right now, and that's about as reliable a September pattern as this zone produces — hi-lo rigs with sandworm or clam, fished in 15 to 25 feet, are filling coolers with fish in the half-pound to pound-and-a-half range. It's not glamorous fishing, but it's honest fishing, and right now it's some of the most consistent action in the zone.

Fluke are still around but the bite has gone patchy the way it does this time of year — some boats working the deeper edges off Sheffield Island are still connecting on keepers with bucktail-and-Gulp combinations dragged slow along the bottom, but plenty of trips are coming back with more shorts than keepers. If fluke is the target, fish the last of an outgoing tide when bait gets pulled off the flats into the channel edges, and don't expect it to be fast. Black sea bass remain a steady, if unspectacular, component mixed in on the same structure that's holding blackfish — squid strips on a standard sea bass rig will pick a few up incidentally while you're working for tog.

Boat traffic is worth a note this week, since the reefs that are producing best — Cockenoe, the western Norwalk Islands, Penfield — are also the ones getting hit hardest by weekend crowds chasing the same blitz reports. Weekday mornings or the first hour of light on weekends will put you on fish with room to work them properly. Looking ahead, the bigger Harvest Moon tides should keep intensifying the bunker-driven blitz pattern through the next few days, and if the albie push that's been working its way west from Fishers Island holds its current pace, this zone's outer edges — the water off Sheffield Island and out toward the open Sound — are the place to watch first. Nothing's confirmed on that yet, but it's the kind of development worth checking before you commit a whole trip to it. For now, the safer bet is the reef pattern already in front of us: bunker at the edges, blackfish and porgies on the structure, and a falling tide that keeps rewarding anyone willing to read it.
